newsitem.title: JAPAN: Big Japan firms urge govt to reform pension system.
newsitem.headline: Big Japan firms urge govt to reform pension system.

text.p: A group of Japan's 71 biggest companies, facing a potential financial squeeze from poorly performing employee pension funds, has urged the government to reform the nation's corporate pension system, an official from the group said on Friday.
"It is possible the credit ratings of Japanese companies will decline if the shortage of pension funds is stated on the companies' balance sheets," the official said.
Japan's rigid pension system should be reformed to help maintain Japanese companies' international competitiveness, he said.

Japan's Welfare Ministry has decided to introduce market value accounting for pension funds' assets from March 1998 to more accurately gauge the financial state of the funds. At present, book value is used to calculate the assets, which does not immediately show losses caused by market price falls.
The official said the 71 firms, including Nippon Steel Corp and Hitachi Ltd, also called for relaxing specified yields to variable yields on pension funds.
Employers participating in the corporate pension system are required to maintain specified yields, currently at 5.5 percent a year, to guarantee predetermined benefits.

However, the actual return on investments is now about three percent as a result of Japan's record low interest rates and weak economic recovery, industry sources said. Many corporate pension funds are facing a shortage of funds to pay benefits to pensioners in the future, they said.
To boost returns on investment, the 71 firms called for the abolition of ceilings setting the maximum level of pension assets that can be invested in different financial instruments.
The official said the group also urged the government to allow them to introduce a defined contribution pension plan, which is popular in the United States, as an option.

In Japan, the benefits that an employee will receive on retirement are set beforehand. Under a defined contribution plan, benefits would depend on how much the employee saved and how well the money had been invested.

Separately, the securities industry has been calling for the introduction of a defined contribution plan, which if it came into effect, would likely see a rise in stock investments through mutual funds such as it is done in the United States, the sources said.
